# Diagnosing Overnight Crank Issues on GM 6.0L V8 Engines

A classic symptom of intermittent fuel or compression issues in heavy-duty applications like the 2008 Cadillac Escalade is a crank that falters immediately after starting, only to stabilize once the engine warms up. The specific behavior describedâcranking for a couple of seconds before slowing down before catching, or taking significantly longer than usualâis a distinct diagnostic signature. It indicates that the engine control unit (ECU) cannot maintain the minimum fuel pressure or air-fuel ratio required to sustain combustion during the initial startup phase when the vehicle is cold.

The hypothesis regarding a leaky injector causing a partial hydrolock is technically sound, but it requires precise verification before replacing expensive components. A hydrolock occurs when liquid enters the cylinder, preventing the piston from completing its compression stroke. Since fuel is incompressible, this creates immediate backpressure that stalls the starter motor or causes the RPM to drop sharply. However, a hydrolock typically prevents startup entirely rather than allowing the engine to run for two seconds and then stumble. A more likely culprit for the "stumble after warm-up" behavior is an injector leaking internally while cold, causing excessive fuel dilution in the oil or cylinder walls, which washes away protective films on piston rings or leads to a flooded condition that the ECU struggles to clear.

The fact that there are no engine codes is actually a strong diagnostic clue. Modern OBD-II systems generally do not set a Check Engine Light for minor fuel trim adjustments or slight vacuum leaks until the deviation from target air-fuel ratio exceeds a certain threshold, often around 10% to 15%. If the injector leak is marginal or intermittent based on temperature, the ECU may simply be compensating with rich/lean fuel trims without triggering a fault code. The rough idle mentioned supports the theory of uneven cylinder performance; if one bank is slightly flooded due to a leaking injector, that cylinder will misfire intermittently until the excess fuel burns off during operation.

Before assuming a mechanical failure like a hydrolock or blown head gasket, you must rule out electrical resistance issues in the starter circuit. The user has already replaced the main battery cables, which is the correct first step for voltage drop testing. However, the issue may lie in the high-load condition of the starter motor itself. When an engine sits overnight, internal corrosion on the starter brushes or a weak solenoid can cause high resistance under load. The initial cranking attempt draws maximum current; if the system voltage sags below the threshold required for full RPM, the starter slows down, creating the "slow crank" effect seen in the footage. Once the engine fires and mechanical load changes, the electrical demand shifts, and the engine might catch anyway.

To isolate this without disassembling the engine, perform a direct voltage test at the starter solenoid during a no-start event. Use a digital multimeter to measure battery voltage while cranking. If the voltage drops below 9.6 volts, the starter is likely undersized or failing, regardless of battery health. In many GM vehicles from this era, the starter motor is known to wear out the internal contacts over time, leading exactly to the symptoms of a long crank that eventually clears once the engine fires.

If electrical resistance checks are clean, the next step is to verify fuel pressure retention. A failing fuel pump check valve or a leaking injector will allow pressure to bleed off completely when the key is turned off. Without residual pressure in the rail, the ECU must spin the fuel pump longer just to build baseline pressure before injection can begin. This manifests as an extended crank time. Disconnecting the fuel pressure regulator and checking for leaks at the injectors with a known-good pressure gauge will confirm if an injector is dripping internally or externally while cold.

There is also the possibility of a vacuum leak affecting idle quality, though this rarely causes a hard start unless the intake manifold gasket is severely compromised on one bank specifically. The brake pedal switch codes are unrelated to engine management and can be ignored for this diagnosis. If the issue persists after verifying electrical draw and fuel pressure retention, mechanical inspection of the cylinder head for warping or leaking valves becomes necessary, but that is a last resort after simpler electrical and fuel system checks fail.
